p01.question: A slide reads “94.7% accuracy, ready for launch”. What is the most useful question to ask?
options: Which algorithm produced that number, and can we try a stronger one
What decision does this prediction drive, and what does each kind of mistake cost us
How long did training take and how much did the compute cost
Can the team get it above 97% before we commit to a date
p01.explanation: Accuracy alone says nothing about the product. The decision and the cost of each error direction are what determine the threshold, the metric to optimise and whether the feature is worth shipping — and they are the product manager's to supply, not the team's.

p01.question: Why is “the model must not make mistakes” an acceptance criterion no team can satisfy?
options: Because models are new technology and will improve later
Because the training data always contains errors
Because a working model is wrong on a known share of cases by design, so the criterion has to name how often and in which direction
Because mistakes can only be counted after a full year of operation
p01.explanation: Being wrong is not a defect to be removed; it is a property of a probabilistic system. A criterion that forbids it can never be met, so the team will quietly reinterpret it instead of telling you — which is worse than an honest error budget.

p01.question: Fraud is 0.8% of transactions. A model answers “not fraud” every single time. What does accuracy report?
options: 99.2%, and it catches nothing — accuracy hides how rare the event is
0.8%, because it misses every fraud case
50%, because there are two possible answers
It cannot be computed without a threshold
p01.explanation: With a rare event the majority answer scores brilliantly while being useless. This is the single most common way an impressive number survives a review it should not have survived.

p01.question: A model outputs 0.83 that a transaction is fraud. Who decides whether 0.83 blocks the payment?
options: The model — the threshold is part of its training
The ML engineer, since it is a technical parameter
Nobody: 0.5 is the industry standard and is used as is
The product manager, because moving it trades one cost against another
p01.explanation: The threshold decides how many honest customers you block in order to catch how much fraud. That is a business trade with money on both sides, not a technical default — and 0.5 is a default nobody chose.

p01.question: The team reports a strong offline metric. What does that entitle you to say?
options: That the feature is ready for release
That the candidate is worth an experiment on live traffic
That the business metric will improve by a similar margin
That the model will hold its quality for at least a year
p01.explanation: Offline numbers filter candidates; only an experiment on real traffic tells you what the feature does to the business. Treating the filter as the verdict is how features ship that look good and change nothing.

p02.question: “Block an order over 100,000 if the account is less than a day old.” Rule or model?
options: A model — fraud patterns change constantly
A model, because the amount threshold should be learned from data
A rule — the condition is a complete sentence, it is stable, and every block can be explained
Neither: the request needs to be rejected as too risky
p02.explanation: Written down, the condition is complete and checkable, and it does not drift. It also has to be explainable to the blocked customer, which pushes further toward a rule. Days of work instead of weeks, and auditable by anyone.

p02.question: Which signal says a rule has outlived itself and the problem has become model-shaped?
options: It needs a new exception nearly every week and nobody can predict the next one
It has grown past fifty lines of code
A competitor has announced they use machine learning for it
The team finds it boring to maintain
p02.explanation: Length is not the signal — edit frequency is. Unpredictable weekly exceptions mean the condition is no longer knowable in advance, which is exactly what a model is for. Usefully, the exception log you have been keeping is your labelled training data.

p02.question: Which set of costs does a first sprint estimate for a model typically leave out?
options: Server capacity and the cost of the programming language
Design review and copywriting
The price of the training data licence only
Data that exists at decision time, weeks rather than days, permanent upkeep, and the burden of explaining an answer
p02.explanation: None of these show up in the first sprint, and all of them are permanent. The upkeep in particular never ends: someone owns retraining, monitoring and the pager for as long as the feature lives.

p02.question: “Email anyone who has not opened the app in 30 days.” What is the right response?
options: A model, since predicting app opens requires learning from behaviour
The email itself is a rule; the interesting problem hiding inside it is choosing whom it is worth contacting
A rule, and there is no further question worth asking
Decline it: mass email is not a product feature
p02.explanation: The trigger is trivially a rule. The valuable reframing is that whom to contact — and with what offer — is a churn problem a model already solves. Finding the better question inside a weak request is most of the job.

p02.question: What makes “we are not using ML for that” land as a decision rather than a refusal?
options: Citing the team's capacity for the quarter
Escalating to the CTO so the answer carries authority
Offering the faster alternative and naming the condition that would make you revisit — and owning the watch for it
Promising to reconsider it next planning cycle
p02.explanation: A comparison gives the requester something now; a named trigger shows the decision is reversible on evidence rather than on rank; taking the watch yourself means they do not have to keep pushing. Capacity is true but sounds like a queue.

p03.question: A stakeholder asks for “a model that makes our search smarter”. What has to be filled in before this can enter a roadmap?
options: A budget and a target launch date
A decision on which model architecture to use
The four slots: what the prediction is about, at what moment it is made, which decision it changes, and who acts on it
A benchmark taken from a competitor's search
p03.explanation: “Smarter” is a wish, not a specification. Until the object, the moment, the decision and the actor are named, there is nothing for a team to build and nothing for you to measure — and no way to tell whether the result was worth the quarter.

p03.question: Which of these is stated as a decision rather than a wish?
options: When the results page renders, we re-rank the top 50 candidates, and the customer sees a different order
Search should understand what the customer means
Search relevance should improve quarter over quarter
We should use embeddings to represent queries
p03.explanation: A decision says what changes, for whom, and at what moment. The second and third options describe a desirable state with no action attached; the fourth is an implementation choice, which is the team's to make, not the brief's.

p03.question: A team ships a model whose output appears only on an internal dashboard that nobody has the authority to act on. What has gone wrong?
options: The model is not accurate enough to be trusted
The dashboard needs better visual design
The predictions should have been written to a database instead
No decision was attached to the prediction, so the model changes nothing however good it is
p03.explanation: This is the dashboard failure mode. A prediction with no decision behind it produces a number somebody looks at, not an outcome. Accuracy is irrelevant here: at 99% it would still change nothing.

p03.question: Why does “at what moment” matter as much as “what do we predict”?
options: Because the model has to be retrained on that schedule
Because the moment fixes which data exists yet and how much latency the prediction is allowed
Because it determines which team owns the feature
Because predictions made at the wrong time of day are less accurate
p03.explanation: The moment is a hard constraint on both sides. It decides which features are legitimately available (module P4's point-in-time trap) and what the latency budget is — a prediction that needs 400 ms cannot sit in a path that has 50.

p03.question: Three framings of “make search smarter” are on the table and one of them can be shipped as a rule. Why start there?
options: It delivers the decision and the interface change immediately, and it becomes the baseline the model has to beat
Because rules are always more accurate than models on search problems
Because the ML team is busy with other work this quarter
Because rules need no data
p03.explanation: Shipping the rule first tests the part most likely to be wrong — that anyone acts differently because of the prediction — at a fraction of the cost. It also produces the number the model will be judged against, which is the subject of module P10.

p04.question: A feature is about to enter the roadmap. Which unanswered data question most often kills it later?
options: Whether the data is stored in the same format across systems
Whether the label — the thing you want to predict — is recorded anywhere at all
Whether the warehouse has enough disk space
Whether the data is refreshed daily or hourly
p04.explanation: Features are usually plentiful and labels are not. A project with inputs but no recorded outcome has no way to learn, and discovering that after the commitment turns a quarter into a data-collection project nobody scheduled.

p04.question: At checkout you want to predict whether a delivery will be late. Which of these fields may NOT be used as a feature?
options: The customer's city, taken from the order
The courier's average delay over the previous month
The number of items in the basket
The warehouse dispatch time, which is recorded two hours after the order is placed
p04.explanation: The dispatch time does not exist at checkout, so the live model would never have it. Training on it produces an excellent offline score and a useless production model — the point-in-time trap, and the most common cause of a result that does not survive launch.

p04.question: What does “the label may come from the future, but the features may not” mean in practice?
options: You learn the answer after the fact, which is fine; but every input must have existed at the moment the prediction is made
Labels should be collected before any features are engineered
Historical data is unusable for training and only live data counts
Features have to be recomputed every time a new label arrives
p04.explanation: That asymmetry is the whole rule. The outcome is by definition known later — that is what makes it a label. The inputs are bound to the moment of the decision, and any that are not leak information the model will not have in production.

p04.question: Which label source is usually the cheapest and the most trustworthy, when it exists?
options: Manual annotation by a contracted team
A label inferred by another model
An outcome the product already records as a side effect of normal operation
A survey sent to customers after the fact
p04.explanation: A refund, a cancellation, a click, a chargeback — the product writes these down anyway, at full volume and without anyone's opinion in the middle. Annotation costs money per item and carries the annotator's judgement; a model-inferred label teaches the new model the old model's mistakes.

p04.question: The data exists for 30% of orders — the ones placed through the mobile app. What follows?
options: The project is impossible and should be cancelled
You can safely extrapolate the model to the other 70%
Coverage does not matter as long as the sample is large enough
The feature can launch for mobile orders only, and that limit belongs in the brief rather than in a post-launch surprise
p04.explanation: Partial coverage is a scope statement, not a blocker. What makes it dangerous is discovering it after the promise: the model has simply never seen the other channel, so its numbers there are unknown rather than merely worse.

p05.question: What is the three-metric chain?
options: A business metric, an online proxy you can move within a test, and an offline metric the team optimises — each linked to the one above it
Accuracy, precision and recall, always reported together
A daily, a weekly and a monthly dashboard
One metric per team: product, engineering and finance
p05.explanation: The chain exists because the metric that matters moves too slowly to steer by and the metric the team can optimise means nothing to the business. The proxy in the middle is what connects a model improvement to a result somebody cares about.

p05.question: Why is accuracy a poor KPI for a product review?
options: Because it is hard to compute reliably
Because executives do not understand percentages
Because nobody outside the team can act on it, and it can rise while the business metric falls
Because it changes every time the model is retrained
p05.explanation: Accuracy is an internal instrument, useful to the team tuning the model. As a KPI it hides which error got better, and a model can gain a point of accuracy by becoming more cautious in exactly the cases that made money.

p05.question: Treating the chain as “a testable claim” means what?
options: The chain is validated by asking more stakeholders whether they agree
You are asserting that moving the offline metric moves the proxy, and the proxy moves the business metric — and an experiment can prove you wrong
Each metric has to be tested by a separate team
The chain should be rewritten every quarter regardless of results
p05.explanation: Written down as a claim, the chain becomes falsifiable: if the offline metric improves and the proxy does not, the link is wrong and you have learned something real. Written down as a list of metrics, it just decorates the document.

p05.question: Why name one deciding number before the experiment runs?
options: Because finance requires a single figure for forecasting
Because more than one metric cannot be measured in the same test
Because a model can only be optimised against a single objective
Because deciding afterwards lets you pick whichever metric happened to move, which is how a failed test becomes a launch
p05.explanation: Naming it in advance is what makes the result binding. With five metrics and no commitment, something will always be up, and the review turns into a search for the friendliest chart rather than a decision.

p05.question: What is a guardrail metric for?
options: To replace the primary metric if that one does not move
To give every stakeholder a metric they own
To catch the damage a win might be hiding — it does not need to improve, it must not get worse
To measure the model's technical performance in production
p05.explanation: Guardrails exist because a feature can win on its own metric and lose overall: clicks up, revenue flat, complaints up. They are set as limits, not targets, and one of them breaking is a reason not to ship even when the primary number is good.

p06.question: Risk wants an aggressive fraud threshold, Support wants a conservative one. What settles the argument?
options: Whichever side escalates to the CTO first
Splitting the difference between the two proposals
A more accurate model, which removes the trade-off
A number on each of the two errors, so the trade can be calculated instead of argued
p06.explanation: Both sides are describing a real cost, so neither can win on conviction. A better model shifts the whole curve but never removes the choice: at any accuracy, some threshold still has to be picked, and that is a product decision made of two prices.

p06.question: What does moving the threshold actually do?
options: It makes the model more accurate at the cost of latency
It trades misses for false alarms — it cannot reduce both
It changes how often the model is retrained
It removes the need to price the errors
p06.explanation: The threshold does not touch the model's quality. It slides along a fixed trade-off, choosing which of the two mistakes you would rather make and how often — which is why it belongs to whoever owns the consequences, not to whoever trained the model.

p06.question: A threshold produces 900 alerts a day and the review team can handle 500. What is the effect?
options: The model catches 80% more fraud than it would at 500 alerts
The extra alerts are processed more slowly but remain useful
A backlog forms and the oldest alerts age past usefulness, so the extra 400 catch almost nothing
The review team's accuracy improves with volume
p06.explanation: Detection only counts once somebody acts on it. Past the team's capacity the queue grows without limit and alerts are reviewed after the money has moved, so the threshold is set by the cost ratio and the capacity to act together.

p06.question: How precise do the two error costs need to be?
options: An order of magnitude is usually enough — what matters is which way the asymmetry runs and roughly by how much
Accurate to the cent, or the threshold will be wrong
They need no numbers at all; a qualitative ranking is sufficient
They must be recalculated for every individual transaction
p06.explanation: When one error costs forty times the other, the second decimal place changes nothing and the ratio changes everything. A rough, written-down estimate also has a property that a qualitative ranking lacks: somebody can disagree with it and bring a better number.

p06.question: An error carries a serious safety or reputational consequence that cannot honestly be priced. What do you do?
options: Estimate a figure large enough to dominate the arithmetic
State that this error is not being traded against money, set a floor you will not ship above, and record it as a policy decision
Leave the threshold to the ML team, since it is no longer a product question
Drop the feature, because the trade-off cannot be computed
p06.explanation: An invented figure looks like analysis and can be renegotiated by anyone with a spreadsheet. A stated limit cannot: it says this is a constraint, not a variable. Module P18 works through how to document that.
